records.place: Near Vicuña, Elqui Valley, Coquimbo, Chile

wine.name: Reserva Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah alone, by the house's own sheet.
wine.sites: The family's vineyards along the Elqui Valley, the dry northern valley of the Coquimbo region where vines drink from the river, from near Vicuña down towards the coast.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small boxes, destemmed and crushed, then fermented in stainless steel and taken through its malolactic fermentation. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques for some months, eight in the 2018 vintage by its importers' sheets, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry and plum over black pepper, black olive tapenade and violet, with a smoky, meaty edge; ripe and full in the mouth but held by fresh acidity, with firm, fine tannin.
wine.ageing: Open and generous within two or three years of the vintage, it keeps its pepper and fruit for six to eight years from a good vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour if you like; a large Syrah or Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Used here for the house's barrique aged Syrah, a step above its plainest wines.
Chile's northern valley of the Coquimbo region, long known for pisco grapes before fine wine.

records.table: Viña Falernia's Reserva Syrah comes from the Elqui, Chile's northern valley of pisco grapes and clear skies. It smells of blackberry, black pepper and olive tapenade, with fresh acidity under the ripe fruit: a red for grilled lamb.
records.story: The Elqui was pisco country long before it was wine country: a narrow, dry valley climbing from La Serena into the Andes, planted for brandy and table grapes. The family behind Falernia came to the Elqui from the Alpine village of Dimaro in the Trentino in 1951, by the accounts of guides and the Vicuña tourist office, and in the 1970s one of them began to grow pisco grapes near Vicuña and later to distil. In 1998 he and a cousin, a winemaker from the Trentino, founded Viña Falernia to see whether the valley could make wine rather than spirit, and the cousin made the wines from the start. The Syrah, grown on vineyards from near Vicuña down towards the coast, proved the point: peppery, fresh and ripe at once, it gave the valley a wine name abroad. In 2005 the founder's son began Mayu, a separate winery of the family whose wines are made in the Falernia cellar, and the house added single vineyard Syrah from its Titón vineyard nearer the coast. The Reserva Syrah opens the far north of Chilean wine to a guest: a valley of sun tempered by altitude and the cold Pacific, and a Syrah that tastes of it.

The plan leaves the label open; the Reserva Syrah is chosen because it is the Syrah critics and merchants have listed across many vintages (Decanter, wine.com from 2006, a wine writer's site for 2010 and 2011); the Gran Reserva and Titón go in others.

The eight months in barrique is the 2018 sheet of Enotria and Coe and a UK merchant; the Gran Reserva 2021 sheet gives only part of the wine in barrel for six months, so the making is told by vintage.
The glass rests on Decanter's 2010 note (tapenade, black pepper, dark fruit) and a wine writer's 2011 note (black olive tapenade, violets, bacon fat).
Both founders are living and are described, not named.

wine.name: Tococo
wine.grapes: Syrah, alone in some vintages and with a little Petite Sirah in others.
wine.sites: A single vineyard planted in 2009 at about 1,788 metres in the upper Elqui, on sandy, decomposed granite of the Andes strewn with boulders.
wine.making: Whole bunches are fermented with their own wild yeasts in stone lagares, trodden by foot and with short macerations, and pressed in the old way. The wine is then aged about twenty months, eighteen to twenty two by vintage, in large wooden foudres of 2,500 litres.
wine.glass: Black plum, blueberry and blackberry over cracked pepper, olive tapenade and a flinty note of crushed granite; taut and fresh, with fine, well defined tannin.
wine.ageing: Tight when young and more open after five years or so; it should keep for well over a decade.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a large Syrah glass.

label.means: The single vineyard Syrah of the house, named after the tococo, a small ground bird of northern and central Chile.

records.table: Tococo is the single vineyard Syrah of Viñedos de Alcohuaz, grown on granite at about 1,800 metres in the upper Elqui and trodden by foot in stone lagares. It is peppery, flinty and fresh, so give it time and air.
records.story: Alcohuaz is a hamlet near the head of the Elqui, where the valley narrows into the Andes and the slopes are boulders and sandy granite. A family planted its first vines there in 2005, the La Era parcel by the house's account, and a winemaker joined the family as a partner in the project. The vineyards run from about 1,650 metres to over 2,200, high even for the Andes valleys of Chile. Rhu, a Syrah led blend from several parcels, was the first wine, with the 2011 vintage. The cellar works in the old way: short macerations, wild yeasts and stone lagares in which the grapes are trodden and pressed by foot, then long ageing in large foudres rather than small barrels. Tococo comes from a single parcel planted in 2009 at about 1,788 metres, named after a small ground bird of the valley, and its first vintage was 2015: the house's purest reading of Syrah on granite. Here altitude, rather than the sea, shapes Chile's north: sun and cold nights, and a Syrah of tension and stone.

wine.name: Talinay Chardonnay
wine.sites: The Talinay vineyard, about 12 kilometres from the Pacific at some 150 metres, beside the Fray Jorge reserve, on porous, fractured limestone of an ancient marine terrace lifted to the surface, under the morning fog.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small boxes of 20 kilos, the grapes are fermented and aged in French oak barrels of several forests, Fontainebleau, Jupille and the Vosges among them, for ten or eleven months by the house's sheets for the 2022, with the lees stirred, before bottling.
wine.glass: Lime zest, green apple and crunchy pear over wet chalk and crushed seashells, with a salty, maritime edge and a faint nuttiness from the oak; linear and racy, with a long, fresh finish.
wine.ageing: Bright and taut on release, it gains texture over three to five years and should keep for eight or so.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The coastal vineyard of the house, on marine limestone near the Fray Jorge reserve.
The valley of the Coquimbo region around Ovalle, cooled by the Pacific and its morning fog.

records.table: Old marine limestone about 12 kilometres from the Pacific gives Tabalí its Talinay Chardonnay in the Limarí. Lime zest, green apple and wet chalk meet a salty edge; pour it cool with oysters or ceviche.
records.story: Tabalí takes its name from the old Hacienda Santa Rosa de Tabalí, in the Limarí Valley west of Ovalle, beside the Valle del Encanto, whose rocks carry petroglyphs of the El Molle people. A Chilean businessman of the Luksic family bought the hacienda in the early 1990s and planted its first vineyards in 1993, by the house's own account. The first Tabalí wines reached the market in 2002, and in 2004 the house built its modern cellar. The decisive step came in 2009, when, after years of geological study by the house's account, Tabalí acquired the Talinay vineyard: a raised terrace of marine limestone about 12 kilometres from the sea, rare ground in Chile, beside the Fray Jorge reserve and under the morning fog the Chileans call camanchaca. Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Sauvignon Blanc from Talinay became the wines the house is known by, and a parcel with more lime yet gives the Talinay Caliza. In the glass the Talinay Chardonnay makes the Limarí's case: a desert valley turned cool by the Pacific, and limestone giving Chilean Chardonnay a chalky, saline cut.

wine.name: T.H. Chardonnay
wine.sites: A small vineyard at Quebrada Seca on the northern bank of the Limarí river, in the west of the valley about 21 kilometres from the Pacific by the house's sheet, nearer the sea and its fog than the vineyards around Ovalle.
wine.making: Fermented in egg shaped concrete tanks and French oak barrels, a small share of them new in recent sheets, then aged about ten months on its lees with regular stirring; in the 2022 about seven tenths stayed in concrete, so the oak stays in the background.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and pear over flint, steely notes and fresh bread, with a touch of hazelnut; piercing acidity and a creamy, salty texture on the finish.
wine.ageing: Lively on release, it fills out over three to five years and should keep for six or so.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Quebrada Seca, in the west of the Limarí near the sea, gives the old Maipo house of Undurraga its T.H. Chardonnay. Made largely in concrete eggs, it tastes of lemon, green apple and flint with piercing acidity.
records.story: Undurraga began in the Maipo: its founder planned the winery between 1879 and 1883, by the house's own history, and in 1885 founded it at Talagante, south west of Santiago, naming the estate Fundo Santa Ana after his wife; the house dates its opening harvest to 1891, made by a French winemaker. For generations the founding family ran the house. In 2006 the family sold its holding, and the new owners invested in vineyards and cellars across Chile. The house's Terroir Hunter range, T.H. on the label, gathers small lots of single varieties from the sites the house judged truest to them, from Leyda to the Limarí. Its Limarí Chardonnay comes from Quebrada Seca, a sector on the western side of the valley, on the northern bank of the river about 21 kilometres from the Pacific, nearer the sea than the vineyards around Ovalle. It shows how Chile's large houses have come to work: an old Maipo name sending its winemakers north to the fog and lime of the Limarí for a Chardonnay of flint and acidity rather than warmth.

wine.name: 20 Barrels Limited Edition Syrah
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with a little Cabernet Sauvignon and in some vintages a touch of Carmenère.
wine.sites: The house's Los Almendros estate in the Limarí Valley, on poor alluvial and colluvial soils under cloudless skies with very little rain.
wine.making: Aged about sixteen to seventeen months, in the 2017 vintage half in French oak barriques from a single cooperage, half of them new, and half in large foudres, before the blend is made and bottled.
wine.glass: Blackberry, plum and violet over cracked black pepper, clove and a smoky, tarry note; juicy and fresh in the mouth, with a long, meaty finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable after three or four years, it keeps for ten or so from a good vintage.

records.table: Cono Sur, a Colchagua house, looks north to its Los Almendros estate in the Limarí for the 20 Barrels Syrah. Blackberry, violet and cracked pepper ride on fresh acidity, a match for lamb or a peppered steak.
records.story: Cono Sur, named for the Southern Cone of South America, was created by Concha y Toro in 1993 as a house for new and more adventurous wines, with its cellar at Chimbarongo in the Colchagua Valley. It made its name with Pinot Noir. In 1996 the team set aside twenty barrels of Casablanca Pinot Noir of that year, and the 20 Barrels range was born; the range later grew to wines of several grapes, each from the valley the house judged right for it. For Syrah it looked north, to its Los Almendros estate in the Limarí, and the 20 Barrels Syrah has been listed from that valley in vintages from 2008 onwards. The Limarí suits it: the sun is fierce, but the Pacific and its fog keep the nights cool, and Syrah keeps its pepper and freshness. Two lessons sit in the bottle: a large house choosing a valley for each grape, and the Limarí, known chiefly for Chardonnay, also making a Syrah of perfume and spice.
